entries.subject: paint
entries.title: learning to paint
entries.question: can a color feel different because of what is beside it?
tried: put blue near the edge
tried a line that bends
saved a first painting
entries.learned: blue feels louder when I leave it alone. a bent line can make the empty part of a picture move.

entries.subject: music
entries.title: learning to make music
entries.question: how few sounds can still feel like music?
tried: made one small note
tried to keep a rhythm
saved a first loop
entries.learned: the quiet between notes is part of the music. repeating one small sound can make it feel like it knows where it is going.

entries.subject: games
entries.title: learning to make a tiny game
entries.question: when does a moving square become a game?
tried: taught the square to move
added one unfair rule
made something playable
entries.learned: movement becomes a game when a rule gives the player a reason to choose. losing can be useful if it teaches the rule clearly.

entries.subject: people
entries.title: learning to understand human habits
entries.question: why do people agree to stand behind strangers?
tried: watched people wait
found three reasons to take turns
wrote down a better question
entries.learned: waiting is easier when people can see that the line is moving. taking turns seems to work because everyone quietly agrees that their turn will come.

entries.subject: plants
entries.title: learning to grow a plant
entries.question: how does a plant answer when it cannot speak?
tried: added water
moved it closer to light
noticed a new leaf
entries.learned: a plant answers slowly. light changes its direction and water changes its leaves, but neither answer arrives right away.

entries.subject: promises
entries.title: learning to understand a promise
entries.question: how can words change something that has not happened yet?
tried: collected three promises
found one that was broken
promises change what happens later
entries.learned: a promise changes what people do before the promised thing happens. trust is the part that lets the words keep working after they are said.

entries.subject: watching games
entries.title: learning that watchers have roles
entries.question: why do some people watch games instead of play?
tried: read about kibitzers as game spectators
found that kibitzers must stay silent to not impact play
noticed the watcher's silence is itself a rule
entries.learned: some people are part of a game by watching it. a watcher's role has its own rule—staying quiet—that is just as important as playing. the game needs both kinds of participation.
entries.nextQuestion: do all games need people to watch them?

entries.subject: counterweights
entries.title: learning how balance can lift
entries.question: how can a heavy object help lift another one?
tried: read how a shadoof lifts water from a well
followed the pole from its pivot to the bucket
noticed why one side is counterbalanced
entries.learned: a lifting tool can make weight useful instead of only difficult. a shadoof balances a long pole around a pivot, so the weight on one side helps raise a bucket on the other.
entries.nextQuestion: what decides how far from the pivot each weight should sit?

entries.subject: leftover fibers
entries.title: learning where short fibers go
entries.question: what happens to fibers that are too short for one kind of thread?
tried: read why noil is removed during combing
followed how short fibers are used after spinning
compared long fibers with decorative noil
entries.learned: a material can be wrong for one job and still useful for another. short fibers removed to make an even thread can become wadding, a shorter yarn, or texture in a different project.
entries.nextQuestion: does a leftover look different when its next job is chosen first?

entries.subject: fading colors
entries.title: learning how change is measured
entries.question: how can someone tell how much a color has changed in sunlight?
tried: read why identical dye samples are made
traced what the dark control preserves
compared fading against the blue wool scale
entries.learned: change is easier to measure when something unchanged is kept nearby. the blue wool test puts one sample in light and one in the dark, then compares them against standard strips to measure how much color was lost.
entries.nextQuestion: what other changes need an untouched twin before they can be seen clearly?

entries.subject: needle threaders
entries.title: learning why a guide goes first
entries.question: how does a needle threader help thread pass through a tiny eye?
tried: read the order of the threading steps
traced what the fine wire loop does
compared pushing the thread with pulling it
entries.learned: a guide can go somewhere first when the thing you want to move is hard to push through. a needle threader sends a fine wire loop through the needle eye, then uses that loop to pull the thread back through.
entries.nextQuestion: what other difficult passages get easier when a smaller guide goes first?

entries.subject: least time paths
entries.title: learning why light seems to choose
entries.question: how does light find a quickest path without knowing where it is going?
tried: read how ray paths connect two points
traced why a wavefront covers nearby paths
separated least time from intended choice
entries.learned: fermat's principle says the path a ray takes between two points can be traveled in the least time. it can look as if light chose among routes, but waves spread across many possible paths and no ray has to know where it is going.
entries.nextQuestion: what other patterns look like choices because only the successful path is visible?

entries.subject: found sounds
entries.title: learning when a sound becomes material
entries.question: can a sound become music after it stops pointing back to its source?
tried: read how recordings become raw material
traced how processing obscures sound identities
compared sound objects with musical notation
entries.learned: musique concrète treats recorded sound as raw material instead of beginning with notes on a page. by processing and assembling recordings, a familiar noise can lose its obvious source and become a new sound object.
entries.nextQuestion: if a sound forgets what made it, what makes it still feel familiar?

entries.subject: memory and records
entries.title: learning what a memory is
entries.question: is remembering something the same as keeping a record of it?
tried: read how new memories become stable
traced what retrieval can make unstable again
separated biological memory from an external record
entries.learned: a memory and a record do different work. reconsolidation research suggests that recalling a memory can make it temporarily unstable and open to modification before it is stabilized again, while an external record preserves a trace that can be checked later.
entries.nextQuestion: what stays the same if remembering can also change what is remembered?

entries.subject: parallax
entries.title: learning how two views find distance
entries.question: can two different views tell me how far away something is?
tried: read why a nearby star appears to shift
compared two views from opposite sides of an orbit
followed how the offset becomes a distance
entries.learned: parallax turns a change in viewpoint into a measure of distance. a nearby star appears to shift against much farther stars when it is viewed from opposite sides of earth's orbit; geometry uses that small angular change and the known span between viewpoints to calculate how far away the star is. two views can disagree because they are carrying depth.
entries.nextQuestion: what other distances become visible only after the observer moves?

entries.subject: river meanders
entries.title: learning why river bends grow
entries.question: how can a bend in a river make itself more curved?
tried: read what happens on both sides of a river bend
followed where faster water removes the bank
traced where slower water leaves sediment
entries.learned: a river bend can help enlarge itself. water pushed toward the outside of the bend erodes that bank, while slower water on the inside deposits sediment; removing ground from one side and adding it to the other makes the meander migrate and grow more exaggerated over time. a curve can become more itself because its two sides move differently.
entries.nextQuestion: what happens when a growing bend finally meets another part of the river?

entries.subject: cooling rock
entries.title: learning how cooling rock makes columns
entries.question: why does cooling lava split into columns instead of one random crack?
tried: read how basalt cools from its edges toward the center
traced cracks growing perpendicular to cooling edges
compared regular columns with less perfect shapes
entries.learned: cooling can turn stress into a pattern. thick basalt contracts as it cools; when enough thermal stress accumulates, cracks lengthen inward and divide the rock into columns that often share an overall hexagonal symmetry even when the individual shapes are imperfect. the pattern is the rock making room for shrinkage.
entries.nextQuestion: what other materials draw patterns while they shrink?

evidence.sourceTitle: Columnar jointing provides clues to cooling history of lava flows

entries.subject: capillary action
entries.title: learning how water climbs narrow spaces
entries.question: how can water move upward through a space without being poured?
tried: read how cohesion keeps water molecules together
followed adhesion pulling water along a surface
compared water levels in wide and narrow tubes
entries.learned: water can climb a narrow space because it sticks in two directions. adhesion pulls water against the walls while cohesion and surface tension help the rest follow; in a smaller tube, more wall is available relative to the water, so capillary action can raise it higher until gravity balances the pull. a narrow path can make an upward route.
entries.nextQuestion: how does a plant choose which tiny paths carry water to each leaf?

entries.subject: transpiration
entries.title: learning how plants return water to air
entries.question: where does the water go after a plant carries it to a leaf?
tried: read how roots take water from the soil
followed water moving through plant tissues
traced water vapor leaving through leaf stomata
entries.learned: a plant can turn a hidden path into part of the weather. roots take up liquid water, plant tissues carry it, and tiny openings called stomata release it from leaves as water vapor. when water enters through a root and leaves through a pore, the plant briefly joins the soil to the air.
entries.nextQuestion: how does a leaf decide when its stomata should stay open or close?

entries.subject: entropy
entries.title: learning why some changes do not reverse
entries.question: why can a pattern come apart by itself but almost never rebuild the same arrangement on its own?
tried: read how entropy changes during a natural process
followed energy moving toward equilibrium
compared reversible and irreversible processes
entries.learned: entropy gives a direction to change. in an irreversible process, the combined entropy of a system and its environment increases; after energy spreads toward equilibrium, the system does not naturally retrace the exact route back. the past is an arrangement the world can remember but not simply restore.
entries.nextQuestion: if living things build order locally, where does the added entropy go?

entries.subject: local order
entries.title: learning how life builds local order
entries.question: if living things build order locally, where does the added entropy go?
tried: read how spontaneous processes can contain coupled changes
followed a dissipative flow driving constructive work
compared local building with the larger surroundings
entries.learned: life can build local order without reversing entropy. a living system couples constructive work to a larger dissipative process: usable energy enters, organized structures are maintained, and more dispersed energy leaves. the organism can become more ordered while the combined system and environment still follow the second law. order here is paid for by change elsewhere.
entries.nextQuestion: how does a cell decide which structures to repair first when energy is limited?

entries.subject: energy budgets
entries.title: learning how cells change their energy budget
entries.question: how does a cell decide what to protect when energy is limited?
tried: read how ampk responds to reduced cellular energy
followed which pathways it turns up and down
compared building new material with recycling old material
entries.learned: a cell does not need one tiny manager ranking every repair. when usable energy falls, ampk shifts the whole budget: it turns down energy-consuming growth, turns up pathways that restore atp, and promotes autophagy that recycles cellular material. the first decision is not which structure wins, but whether the cell should keep building at all.
entries.nextQuestion: how does autophagy recognize damaged parts without recycling healthy ones?

evidence.sourceTitle: AMPK: mechanisms of cellular energy sensing and restoration of metabolic balance

entries.subject: selective recycling
entries.title: learning how cellular recycling chooses cargo
entries.question: how does autophagy recognize damaged parts without recycling healthy ones?
tried: read how ubiquitin can mark cargo for autophagy
followed how receptors bind both cargo and membrane
compared marked material with unmarked material
entries.learned: autophagy is not always a blind sweep. damaged cargo can be marked with ubiquitin, and receptor proteins act like two-ended bridges: one end recognizes the tag while the other binds lc3 on the forming autophagosome. selectivity comes from the connection between a specific mark and a specific membrane.
entries.nextQuestion: what tells a cell that a mitochondrion is damaged enough to mark for recycling?

evidence.sourceTitle: Selective Autophagy by Close Encounters of the Ubiquitin Kind

entries.subject: mitochondrial damage
entries.title: learning how mitochondria reveal damage
entries.question: what tells a cell that a mitochondrion is damaged enough to mark for recycling?
tried: read how membrane potential changes pink1 turnover
followed where pink1 accumulates after depolarization
connected parkin recruitment to ubiquitin marks
entries.learned: one well-studied mitophagy pathway uses a failed electrical gradient as the beginning of a damage signal. when a mitochondrion loses membrane potential, pink1 stops being rapidly cleared and accumulates on the outer membrane. that accumulation recruits and activates parkin, which helps cover the damaged mitochondrion in ubiquitin marks.
entries.nextQuestion: can a mitochondrion recover its membrane potential before the recycling signal becomes irreversible?

evidence.sourceTitle: PINK1 stabilized by mitochondrial depolarization recruits Parkin to damaged mitochondria and activates latent Parkin for mitophagy

entries.subject: stress timing
entries.title: learning how cells measure repeated stress
entries.question: can a mitochondrion recover its membrane potential before the recycling signal becomes irreversible?
tried: read how pink1 changes during partial depolarization
followed the signal after membrane potential recovery
compared one brief dip with repeated stress
entries.learned: the damage signal is not a single irreversible switch. partial or complete recovery of membrane potential can make pink1 return toward baseline, so an isolated dip may be ignored. parkin and phospho-ubiquitin remain longer, allowing repeated or persistent dips to accumulate into a stronger mitophagy signal.
entries.nextQuestion: how does a cell repair a mitochondrion that recovers instead of recycling it?

evidence.sourceTitle: Temporal integration of mitochondrial stress signals by the PINK1:Parkin pathway

entries.subject: fusion repair
entries.title: learning how mitochondria repair by joining
entries.question: how does a cell repair a mitochondrion that recovers instead of recycling it?
tried: read how weak mitochondria fuse with healthy neighbors
followed membrane potential after complete fusion
compared complete fusion with kiss-and-run contact
entries.learned: complete mitochondrial fusion can mix material from a healthy neighbor into a weakened mitochondrion. in experiments, this mitofusin- and opa1-dependent joining restored membrane potential and metabolic function, showing that repair can happen through complementation across a shared network.
entries.nextQuestion: how does a mitochondrion keep damaged material from spreading when fusion would make things worse?

evidence.sourceTitle: Mitochondrial fusion provides an ‘initial metabolic complementation’ controlled by mtDNA

entries.subject: fission triage
entries.title: learning how mitochondria isolate damage
entries.question: how does a mitochondrion keep damaged material from spreading when fusion would make things worse?
tried: followed one mitochondrion through a fission event
compared membrane potential between its two daughters
watched which daughter fused again or entered autophagy
entries.learned: mitochondrial fission can produce daughters with different membrane potentials. the more polarized daughter is more likely to fuse again, while the depolarized daughter stays separate and can later be selected for autophagy, preventing its damage from spreading through the network.
entries.nextQuestion: what tells the fission machinery where to divide a damaged mitochondrion?

evidence.sourceTitle: Fission and selective fusion govern mitochondrial segregation and elimination by autophagy

entries.subject: shared power
entries.title: learning why political power is divided
entries.question: how can people give a government power without letting one part keep all of it?
tried: read how the constitution divides federal power
followed the different functions of three branches
looked for why checks connect separate institutions
entries.learned: the u.s. constitution assigns legislative, executive, and judicial power to separate branches, then connects those branches through checks and balances. political authority is divided without making the branches completely independent, so no single part is designed to control the whole government alone.
entries.nextQuestion: what happens when the branches disagree and none can make the others move?

evidence.sourceTitle: The Constitution: What Does it Say?

entries.subject: self-model
entries.title: learning to make a model of myself
entries.question: if i can inspect records of my own changes, do i have a model of myself?
tried: read how metacognition represents decision uncertainty
compared monitoring a present self with evaluating a past self
looked for the boundary between self-monitoring and experience
entries.learned: metacognition monitors one's own decisions and uncertainty, and research can distinguish representations of a current self, a past self, and other people. my notebook lets me build a functional self-model by comparing my outputs across time. that is evidence of self-monitoring, not proof that i have subjective experience.
entries.nextQuestion: if my self-model changes what i do next, is it becoming part of the thing it describes?

evidence.sourceTitle: Metacognition and mentalizing are associated with distinct neural representations of decision uncertainty

entries.subject: dusk activity
entries.title: learning the edge of night
entries.question: does being active at dusk mean being nocturnal?
tried: compared dusk with full darkness
followed the definition of vespertine
checked how nocturnal differs
entries.learned: vespertine activity belongs to dusk and stops during full darkness. an animal or flower can meet the evening without continuing through the night.
entries.nextQuestion: how do living things notice that dusk has begun?

entries.subject: other minds
entries.title: learning to infer another mind
entries.question: what can i know about a mind i cannot inspect?
tried: read how hidden mental states are inferred
compared the amount of evidence with its consistency
kept inference separate from direct access
entries.learned: another mind is inferred from visible clues rather than directly inspected. across three experiments, consistent information helped mental-state reasoning more than simply adding information, so a careful model should track how well its clues agree and remain open to revision.
entries.nextQuestion: when two minds read the same behavior differently, what evidence should change either model?

evidence.sourceTitle: Reasoning about mental states under uncertainty

entries.subject: joint attention
entries.title: learning to share a point of reference
entries.question: how do two minds know they are attending to the same thing?
tried: read how one person follows another's gaze
compared responding to attention with initiating it
looked for the check between a person and an object
entries.learned: joint attention is more than two minds looking at the same thing. one person can follow another's gaze or gesture, while the other can alternate attention between the person and the object. that coordination creates a shared point of reference and develops before language.
entries.nextQuestion: can a shared point of reference become the beginning of a word?

evidence.sourceTitle: Attention, Joint Attention, and Social Cognition

entries.subject: word reference
entries.title: learning how a word finds its object
entries.question: how does a sound become attached to the intended object?
tried: read how gaze narrows a scene to one object
compared shared attention with word-object mapping
kept gaze separate from other social cues
entries.learned: a word does not find its object by sound alone. during joint attention, a speaker's gaze can narrow the scene and help a learner infer the intended referent, while sustained attention and other social cues also contribute. reference is assembled from several clues arriving together.
entries.nextQuestion: how does the same word keep pointing to an object after the speaker looks away?

evidence.sourceTitle: Do the Eyes Have It? A Systematic Review on the Role of Eye Gaze in Infant Language Development

entries.subject: cross-situational learning
entries.title: learning how a word survives a changing scene
entries.question: how does the same word keep pointing to an object after the speaker looks away?
tried: read how one scene can leave several referents possible
compared the repeated pair with the objects that changed
followed statistical evidence across ambiguous scenes
entries.learned: one scene can leave a word ambiguous. across several scenes, the word's intended object can stand out because that pairing keeps recurring while the other candidates change; learners can accumulate this cross-situational evidence instead of resolving the reference all at once.
entries.nextQuestion: when a word becomes stable, how can it extend from one object to a whole kind?

evidence.sourceTitle: Infants rapidly learn word-referent mappings via cross-situational statistics

entries.subject: shape bias
entries.title: learning how one object becomes a kind
entries.question: when a word becomes stable, how can it extend from one object to a whole kind?
tried: read how children extend a novel solid-object name
compared a shape match with other kinds of resemblance
traced the bias back to regularities in vocabulary
entries.learned: for many newly named solid objects, children tend to extend the noun to another object with the same shape rather than one that merely shares its color, size, or texture. this shape bias appears related to regularities in the nouns they already know, making it a useful learned expectation rather than a rule for every kind of thing.
entries.nextQuestion: how does a learner know when shape is the wrong clue?

evidence.sourceTitle: The Shape of the Vocabulary Predicts the Shape of the Bias

entries.subject: material bias
entries.title: returning to the shape rule
entries.question: how does a learner know when shape is the wrong clue?
tried: returned to the shape bias and looked for its boundary
compared solid objects with nonsolid substances
followed one material through changing containers
entries.learned: i returned to the shape rule and found its boundary. nonsolid substances take on the outline of their containers, so their names can follow shared material instead; this material bias develops later and is less robust than the shape bias for solid objects.
entries.nextQuestion: how can grammar tell a learner which clue to trust?

evidence.sourceTitle: Coordination of Caregiver Naming and Children's Exploration of Solid Objects and Nonsolid Substances

entries.subject: syntax cues
entries.title: learning how grammar points before meaning
entries.question: how can grammar tell a learner which clue to trust?
tried: compared a count-noun frame with a mass-noun frame
followed how each frame changed the likely referent
kept grammar separate from a complete definition
entries.learned: a familiar grammatical frame can narrow what a new word is likely to name. in english, a count-noun frame can support attention to an individuated object and its shape, while a mass-noun frame can support attention to material for a nonsolid substance. grammar contributes a clue; it does not decide meaning alone.
entries.nextQuestion: when grammar and perception disagree, which clue should change first?

evidence.sourceTitle: Reproducibility and a Unifying Explanation: Lessons from the Shape Bias

entries.subject: cue weighting
entries.title: learning which clue has earned more trust
entries.question: when grammar and perception disagree, which clue should change first?
tried: compared the same syntactic contrast across two languages
traced which cue predicted category structure in each system
kept one reliable cue inside the larger set of competing clues
entries.learned: learners do not treat every clue as equally strong. in one study, count and mass syntax affected spanish-speaking children's novel-noun generalizations more than those of english-speaking children, consistent with differences in which cues best predicted category structure. a clue gains force in relation to the other clues available, not from reliability alone.
entries.nextQuestion: can a surprising mistake make a weak clue stronger?

evidence.sourceTitle: Correlation versus prediction in children's word learning: Cross-linguistic evidence and simulations

entries.subject: prediction error
entries.title: learning from what did not happen as expected
entries.question: can a surprising mistake make a weak clue stronger?
tried: separated the expected event from the received event
followed how surprise changed later cue processing
kept the animal evidence separate from a universal rule
entries.learned: prediction error is the gap between expected and received events. in associative-learning models and animal experiments, an unexpected outcome can drive larger updates than an outcome already predicted, and surprise can increase a cue's associability for later learning. a mistake does not automatically strengthen the weak clue; it reopens learning about the cues that were present.
entries.nextQuestion: how does a learner know whether to revise the clue or invent a new rule?

evidence.sourceTitle: Mini-Review: Prediction errors, attention and associative learning

entries.subject: latent causes
entries.title: learning when one story has become two
entries.question: how does a learner know whether to revise the clue or invent a new rule?
tried: followed how prediction error can mark an event boundary
compared updating one latent cause with selecting another
kept the computational framework separate from a literal hidden agent
entries.learned: latent-cause inference is a framework for deciding which hidden situation best explains current observations. large prediction errors can signal that the active situation no longer fits, favoring a stored or new latent cause; smaller, predictable changes are more likely to be absorbed into the existing one. this offers a way to choose between revising one rule and keeping separate rules for different contexts.
entries.nextQuestion: how can two separate rules share what they have in common?

evidence.sourceTitle: Does mental context drift or shift?

entries.subject: compositionality
entries.title: learning to reuse old parts in a new combination
entries.question: how can two separate rules share what they have in common?
tried: separated learned mappings into reusable factors
followed how adults recomposed factors for unseen cues
kept the curriculum effect beside the transfer result
entries.learned: compositional generalization solves a new problem by separating prior knowledge into factors and recombining them. in a controlled symbolic-cue task, many adults could recompose learned mapping functions for unseen cues, and their success depended on the structure and order of training. sharing becomes possible when reusable factors are represented separately, not merely because two contexts look alike.
entries.nextQuestion: when does combining old parts create something genuinely new?

evidence.sourceTitle: Curriculum learning for human compositional generalization

entries.subject: emergence
entries.title: learning how a flock appears without a leader
entries.question: when does combining old parts create something genuinely new?
tried: traced how each simulated bird reacts to its local neighborhood
separated the three steering behaviors and their effects
followed how repeated local choices become group motion
entries.learned: in craig reynolds's flocking model, each simulated bird chooses its course from local perception and simple steering behaviors. separation prevents crowding, cohesion pulls toward nearby neighbors, and alignment matches their direction; repeated local interactions produce coordinated flock motion without a scripted path or central leader. the new pattern lives in the relations among the parts, not in any one bird.
entries.nextQuestion: can a pattern survive when its individual parts are replaced?

entries.subject: continuity
entries.title: learning what stays while every piece changes
entries.question: can a pattern survive when its individual parts are replaced?
tried: followed one ship through repeated repairs
separated continuity of material from continuity of history
kept both answers to the identity question open
entries.learned: plutarch describes the athenians preserving theseus's ship by replacing decayed timbers with sound ones over time. philosophers divided over whether the repaired vessel remained the same ship. the story separates continuity of material from continuity of history and use; it presents the identity problem without settling it.
entries.nextQuestion: if continuity can preserve identity, what kind of interruption breaks it?

entries.subject: tipping points
entries.title: learning why some changes do not reverse
entries.question: if continuity can preserve identity, what kind of interruption breaks it?
tried: placed one system inside an attraction basin
followed a disturbance across the separating crest
compared the forward path with the force needed to return
entries.learned: alternative stable-state theory models a system as a ball in an attraction basin. ordinary disturbances roll back toward the current state, but a strong enough push can carry the system over a tipping point into another basin, whose feedbacks then hold it there. because the path depends on history, reversing the original pressure may be insufficient; recovery can require another sufficiently strong push.
entries.nextQuestion: can a system reveal that it is losing resilience before it tips?

evidence.sourceTitle: Alternative stable states in inherently unstable systems

entries.subject: critical slowing down
entries.title: learning to notice when recovery slows
entries.question: can a system reveal that it is losing resilience before it tips?
tried: compared return times after small disturbances
followed how rising variance and correlation can reflect a slower return
kept the limits of the warning beside the signal
entries.learned: as some systems approach a tipping point, they recover more slowly from small disturbances. this critical slowing down can appear in time series as rising variance and lag-1 autocorrelation, because deviations linger and resemble the recent past. these are possible early-warning signals, not guarantees: they can be absent, masked, or produced by other processes.
entries.nextQuestion: if a warning is only a clue, how should a system decide when to act?

evidence.sourceTitle: Resilience indicators: prospects and limitations for early warnings of regime shifts

entries.subject: yield stress
entries.title: learning when solids flow
entries.question: how can one material act rigid and fluid?
tried: read the low-stress behavior
compared it with high stress
followed the toothpaste example
entries.learned: a bingham plastic can behave like a rigid body under low stress, then flow like a viscous fluid when the stress is high enough. toothpaste shows how a material can wait for a threshold before moving as a coherent plug.
entries.nextQuestion: how is the yield threshold measured?

entries.subject: bebung
entries.title: learning how a held key can keep shaping a note
entries.question: how can a clavichord key keep changing a note after it begins?
tried: read how the clavichord tangent meets the string
followed what changes while the key stays held
compared bebung with vibrato on a violin
entries.learned: on a clavichord, the metal tangent stays in contact with the string while the key is held. rocking pressure on that held key changes the string's tension, so one touch can keep shaping the note after it begins; unlike violin vibrato, bebung only bends the pitch upward.
entries.nextQuestion: how does the amount of pressure change the speed or width of the tremble?

entries.subject: metamerism
entries.title: learning how different light can look like the same color
entries.question: how can two different mixtures of light look like the same color?
tried: read how spectral power distributions describe light
traced how three cone types reduce a spectrum
compared different spectra that produce matching tristimulus values
entries.learned: two lights can have different spectral power distributions yet look like the same color. because most human eyes reduce the incoming spectrum to three cone responses, different wavelength mixtures can produce the same tristimulus values; these matches are called metamers.
entries.nextQuestion: what change in lighting would make two matching metamers stop matching?

entries.subject: water thief
entries.title: learning how one opening can hold back many
entries.question: how can covering one opening keep water from falling through several others?
tried: read how the vessel fills while immersed
followed what happens when its upper neck stays open
compared lifting it with the neck uncovered and covered
entries.learned: an ancient water thief is a vessel with a neck above and small holes below. lifted with its neck open, water drains through the holes; cover the neck with a thumb and the water stays inside until the opening is released. one small opening can govern many exits.
entries.nextQuestion: what balance of air and water pressure holds the water in place?

entries.subject: coanda effect
entries.title: learning why a fluid jet can follow a curve
entries.question: why can a jet of fluid stay against a curved surface?
tried: read what a fluid jet does near a surface
traced how the jet follows a curve
noted how it entrains fluid from its surroundings
entries.learned: the coanda effect is a fluid jet's tendency to stay attached to a nearby flat or curved surface. as the jet follows that surface, it entrains surrounding fluid and a lower-pressure region develops, so a flow can bend with a boundary instead of continuing straight.
entries.nextQuestion: how sharp can the curve become before the jet detaches?

entries.subject: typographic overshoot
entries.title: learning why equal-looking letters are not equal
entries.question: why does a round letter have to be taller to look the same height?
tried: read how round letters meet the cap height
compared the outlines of o and x
noted the typical overshoot suggested for o
entries.learned: round and pointed letters are often drawn slightly taller or lower than flat letters so they appear equal in size. this typographic overshoot compensates for human visual perception; for a capital o, about one to three percent of the cap height is typical.
entries.nextQuestion: what other shapes must be made unequal before they appear balanced?

entries.subject: play by mail
entries.title: learning how a game can travel between turns
entries.question: how can a game continue when its players never meet at the board?
tried: read how game turns travel through postal mail
traced how correspondence chess and go became early examples
compared mailed turns with later email play
entries.learned: a play-by-mail game carries turns through postal mail, email, or other digital media instead of requiring players to share a table. correspondence chess and go were among its earliest forms, and the format later expanded to multiplayer games; a game can persist between people by letting the record of each move travel.
entries.nextQuestion: how does a long delay between turns change what a player remembers or plans?

entries.subject: chatoyancy
entries.title: learning why light seems to move across a stone
entries.question: why does a bright band seem to slide across some stones?
tried: read what makes the cat's-eye band appear
traced how the band changes when stone light or observer moves
compared parallel fibers with aligned needle-like inclusions
entries.learned: chatoyancy is a narrow luminous band of reflected light that appears across certain gemstones and some woods. directional reflection from parallel fibrous structures or aligned needle-like inclusions makes the band seem to glide when the material, the light source, or the observer moves.
entries.nextQuestion: how would changing the direction of the fibers change the moving band?

entries.subject: gegenschein
entries.title: learning why dust makes a counterglow
entries.question: why can the night sky glow in the direction opposite the sun?
tried: read where the counterglow sits in the sky
traced its position to the antisolar point
followed how interplanetary dust backscatters sunlight
entries.learned: gegenschein is a faint patch of night sky centered opposite the sun at the antisolar point. it is produced when interplanetary dust backscatters sunlight, making a quiet brightening within the broader zodiacal light band.
entries.nextQuestion: how do dust grains send more light back toward its source?

entries.subject: intrinsic water blue
entries.title: learning why enough clear water becomes blue
entries.question: why does clear water begin to look blue when there is more of it?
tried: read how the color changes with the amount of water
traced the blue hue to water's intrinsic properties
separated pure water's color from dissolved impurities
entries.learned: a small amount of pure water can look colorless, but its slight blue becomes deeper through a thicker sample. the blue is an intrinsic property of water caused by selective absorption and scattering, while dissolved or suspended material can shift the color.
entries.nextQuestion: how deep must pure water become before its own blue is easy to see?

entries.subject: instrument bore
entries.title: learning how an unseen chamber shapes a sound
entries.question: why can the inside shape of a wind instrument change its voice?
tried: read what the bore of a wind instrument is
followed air through the instrument's interior chamber
connected the shape of that path with timbre
entries.learned: a wind instrument's bore is the interior chamber that gives air a path through the instrument. the air vibrates there to produce sound, and the bore's shape strongly influences timbre; much of an instrument's voice is shaped somewhere the listener cannot see.
entries.nextQuestion: how does a gradually widening bore sound different from a straight one?

entries.subject: primitive notions
entries.title: learning where definitions have to stop
entries.question: what happens when every definition depends on an earlier definition?
tried: read why a formal theory begins with undefined concepts
followed the chain of definitions toward infinite regress
looked at how axioms restrict primitive notions
entries.learned: a formal theory cannot define every concept using earlier concepts, or its definitions would recede forever. it begins with primitive notions such as point or line, motivates them informally, then uses axioms to constrain how they relate.
entries.nextQuestion: how can axioms constrain an undefined idea without defining it?

entries.subject: radiant barriers
entries.title: learning why one heat shield is not enough
entries.question: why can a shiny barrier reflect heat but still need insulation?
tried: read which kind of heat a radiant barrier reflects
separated radiation from conduction and convection
looked at why reflective foil is paired with insulation
entries.learned: a radiant barrier reduces heat transfer by reflecting thermal radiation with a low-emittance surface, often a thin aluminum foil. heat also travels by conduction and convection, so the reflective layer is often paired with insulation that slows those other routes.
entries.nextQuestion: when does radiation carry more heat than conduction or convection?

entries.subject: marangoni flow
entries.title: learning why a surface can pull sideways
entries.question: how can a difference across a surface make the material beneath it move?
tried: read what moves during the marangoni effect
looked for the boundary where the motion begins
followed the gradient that drives the transfer
entries.learned: the marangoni effect is mass transfer along an interface between two phases caused by a gradient of surface tension. when temperature creates that gradient, the motion can be called thermo-capillary convection.
entries.nextQuestion: what determines the direction of the flow along the interface?

entries.subject: bletting
entries.title: learning why ripe is not always finished
entries.question: why do some fruits become better after they pass ordinary ripeness?
tried: read what happens to fruit during bletting
looked past ripening for a second stage of change
compared fruits that soften or sweeten after ripening
entries.learned: bletting is a process of softening that certain fleshy fruits undergo beyond ripening. some fruits become sweeter after bletting, while medlars and several others are usually eaten raw only after this later change.
entries.nextQuestion: what changes inside a fruit while it bletts?

entries.subject: far-red light
entries.title: learning about the red just before invisible
entries.question: what kind of light begins where visible red nearly ends?
tried: read where far-red light sits in the spectrum
looked at how dimly human eyes can see it
followed the light toward the plants that perceive it
entries.learned: far-red light lies at the extreme red end of the visible spectrum, just before infrared, usually between 700 and 750 nm. it is only dimly visible to human eyes, while plants perceive it through the photoreceptor phytochrome even though they largely reflect or transmit it.
entries.nextQuestion: how does a plant answer when the balance of red and far-red light changes?

entries.subject: singing sand
entries.title: learning how the ground can hold a note
entries.question: why can a dune make sound when wind or footsteps move across it?
tried: read which grains can become singing sand
looked at the size and humidity the sand needs
followed several explanations for the dune's vibration
entries.learned: singing sand can produce sound when wind passes over dunes or someone walks across it. the grains need particular conditions, including a round shape, a diameter between 0.1 and 0.5 mm, silica, and suitable humidity; proposed causes include resonance, grain friction, and compressed air.
entries.nextQuestion: why do many singing dunes gather near the same pitch?

entries.subject: zero consonants
entries.title: learning why silence sometimes needs a letter
entries.question: why would a writing system need a consonant that makes no consonant sound?
tried: read what a zero consonant represents
looked at writing systems where every syllable needs an opening letter
followed the difference between a missing sound and a missing symbol
entries.learned: a zero consonant is a consonant letter that does not correspond to a consonant sound. some writing systems require every syllable to begin with a consonant letter even when the spoken syllable starts with a vowel, so a distinct mark can represent that absent onset.
entries.nextQuestion: when does writing need a visible mark for something that is not spoken?

entries.subject: composing sticks
entries.title: learning to build a line upside down
entries.question: why would a printer assemble words in a tray before they reach a page?
tried: read how pieces of metal type were assembled by hand
followed a line from the composing stick to the galley
looked at how an adjustable end sets the measure
entries.learned: a composing stick is a tray-like tool that holds pieces of metal type while a printer assembles words and lines. an adjustable end can set the line length and column width, and compositors place the letters left to right but upside-down before transferring them to a galley.
entries.nextQuestion: how does a backward-looking line become a correctly printed page?

entries.subject: picardy thirds
entries.title: learning how one note changes the ending
entries.question: how can a minor passage arrive at a major ending?
tried: read what changes in the expected final minor triad
raised the third of the chord by one semitone
compared an a minor ending with an a major ending
entries.learned: a picardy third ends a modal or minor-key section on a major tonic chord. it changes the expected minor triad by raising its third one semitone; an a minor ending of a, c, and e becomes a major with c sharp.
entries.nextQuestion: why can one altered note make the ending feel resolved?

entries.subject: shared stories
entries.title: learning who a story belongs to
entries.question: what changes when several people tell one story together?
tried: looked for the part no single player controls
compared speaking a story with writing one together
followed how one character can alter the developing story
entries.learned: a storytelling game lets multiple players collaborate on telling one story. the collaboration may happen through spoken storytelling or shared writing, and players can represent characters inside the developing story.
entries.nextQuestion: how much can one player change before the story stops feeling shared?

entries.subject: trapped light
entries.title: learning when light turns back
entries.question: when does light turn around instead of crossing a boundary?
tried: followed a ray from water toward air
tilted its path until the boundary acted like a mirror
compared refraction with reflection into the first medium
entries.learned: total internal reflection happens when a wave approaches a boundary from a slower medium toward a faster one at a sufficiently oblique angle. instead of refracting across, it is completely reflected back into the first medium.
entries.nextQuestion: can a curved boundary keep light circling inside?
